Your Morning Coffee, Step by Step

A pour-over that tastes like you meant it.

Tune Up a Sluggish Laptop

Most slowness is just clutter wearing a trench coat.

  1. Check storage. Open Settings → System → Storage. If you're above 90% full, that alone can cause lag. Clear Downloads, old installers, and that folder of memes from 2019.

  4. Scan for junk. One quick malware scan with whatever came with your OS. Skip the sketchy "optimizer" apps.
  5. Uninstall unused programs. If you haven't opened it in six months, it's a squatter.
  6. Restart — not sleep, restart. Sleep keeps everything festering.

If it's still slow after all that, the bottleneck is probably the drive. A cheap SSD upgrade is the single biggest speed boost you can buy.

From Seed to Sandwich: Growing Tomatoes

Tomatoes are dramatic, thirsty, and worth it.

  1. Start indoors 6–8 weeks before your last frost. Plant seeds ¼ inch deep in seed-starting mix. Keep soil warm (75°F / 24°C).
  2. Give light. Once sprouts appear, they need 14–16 hours of bright light daily. A south window plus a cheap shop light works.
  3. Harden off over a week: set them outside for an hour, then two, then more. Skipping this shocks them.
  4. Plant deep. Bury the stem up to the top few leaves — tomatoes root along the stem. In-ground or a 5-gallon pot.
  5. Water deeply once or twice a week. Not daily sips. Consistency prevents cracked fruit.
  6. Stake or cage early, before the plant flops over and sulks.
  7. Feed every two weeks once flowers show. Too much nitrogen = all leaves, no fruit.

Pinch off the first yellow flowers if you want a bigger plant before the harvest rush. Feels wrong. Works.

Jump-Start a Car

Dead battery, live friend. Let's get you rolling.

  1. Park close. Nose to nose or side by side. Both engines off. Set parking brakes.
  2. Find the battery. Pop both hoods. Look for the plastic box with two posts. Red is positive (+), black is negative (−).
  3. Connect red first. Clamp one red end to the dead battery's + post. Clamp the other red end to the good battery's + post.
  4. Connect black to good battery. Clamp one black end to the good battery's − post. Clamp the other black end to a bare metal bolt on the dead car's engine block—not the dead battery itself.
  5. Start the good car. Let it run for two minutes. Then try the dead car. If it won't start, wait five more minutes and try again.
  6. Disconnect in reverse. Black off the engine block, black off the good battery, red off the good battery, red off the dead battery. Keep clamps from touching each other.

Careful: Never let red and black clamps touch. If you see sparks when connecting the last black clamp, stop—you're on the wrong spot.

Battery still dead after a drive? It might be time for a new one, user_name.

Unclog a Drain

Before you call a plumber, try these.

  1. Remove the stopper. Lift or unscrew it. Shine a flashlight down. Pull out any hair or gunk with a bent wire or tweezers.
  2. Boiling water. Pour a kettle of hot (not boiling for PVC pipes) water down the drain. Wait five minutes. Repeat.
  3. Baking soda + vinegar. Pour half a cup of baking soda, then half a cup of white vinegar. Cover with a plug. Wait 15 minutes. Flush with hot water.
  4. Plunger. Block the overflow hole with a wet rag. Place the plunger over the drain. Push and pull firmly 15–20 times. Hold the seal.
  5. Drain snake. Feed the auger into the drain. Crank when you feel resistance. Pull it out slowly and wipe the gunk off.
  6. Check the P-trap. Place a bucket under the sink. Unscrew the curved pipe. Clean it out. Reassemble and run water.

If water backs up in other drains too, the clog is deeper. That's a job for a pro.

Back Up Your Computer

The goal: if your laptop vanishes tomorrow, you lose a day, not a decade.

  1. Pick your important stuff. Documents, photos, that folder of tax returns. You don't need to back up the operating system if you have installers or cloud accounts.
  2. Get an external drive. A 1TB or 2TB USB drive is cheap. Plug it in and format it for your system (APFS for Mac, NTFS or exFAT for Windows).
  3. Turn on automatic backups. Mac: Time Machine. Windows: File History or Backup and Restore. Point it at the drive and let it run overnight.
  4. Add a cloud layer. For the irreplaceable stuff — photos, writing, scans — use a cloud service with version history. It's the off-site half of the rule.
  5. Follow 3-2-1. Three copies, on two different media, one off-site. External drive + cloud + the original on your laptop covers it.
  6. Test a restore. Once a year, pull one file back from the backup. A backup you've never restored is a hope, not a plan.
  7. Check it monthly. Open the backup app, confirm the last run succeeded, and glance at free space. Five minutes, big peace of mind.

Change a Car Battery

Ten minutes, one wrench, zero drama. user_name, here's the order.

Steps
  1. Park flat, ignition off, keys in your pocket.
  2. Pop the hood. Find the battery — usually a black brick with two posts, red cover on one.
  3. Loosen the negative terminal (black, marked –) with a 10 mm wrench. Negative first, always.
  4. Loosen the positive terminal (red, +). Tuck both cables aside so they don't spring back.
  5. Unbolt the hold-down clamp at the base of the battery.
  6. Lift the battery straight up. Old ones are heavier than they look.
  7. Set the new battery in, clamp it down, then reconnect positive first, negative last.
  8. Tighten, wiggle-test both posts, and start the car.
Why negative first?

If your wrench touches metal while you're on the positive post, you get a spark. Negative-first means the wrench has nothing to arc to. Boring is safe.

Battery terminals crusty? Scrub with a wire brush and a splash of baking soda water before reconnecting.

Make a Great Cup of Tea

A good cup is mostly about water temperature and not walking away. Here's the flow.

  1. Boil fresh water. Fill the kettle with cold tap water, not reboiled. Reboiled water tastes flat.
  2. Warm the cup. Pour a splash of hot water in, swirl, dump. Keeps your tea hot longer.
  3. Measure the leaves. One teaspoon loose leaf or one bag per 8 oz cup. For strong tea, add a little more leaf, not more time.
  4. Pour at the right temp. Black and herbal: just off boil. Green: 170–180°F. White: 160–170°F. No thermometer? Let boiled water sit 2–3 minutes for green.
  5. Steep. Black 3–5 min, green 2–3 min, white 4–5 min, herbal 5–7 min. Set a timer—oversteeped tea turns bitter fast.
  6. Remove the leaves. Pull the bag or strain. Don't let it sit in the cup.
  7. Add milk or lemon. Milk goes in after pouring for black tea; lemon with green or black, but not both.

If it tastes weak, next time use more leaf, not longer steeping. Bitterness comes from time, strength from quantity.

Jump-Start a Car

Dead battery? You can fix this in five minutes. Order matters—don't skip it.

  1. Park the good car close. Face them hood to hood, engines off. Set both parking brakes. Keep cars from touching.
  2. Find the batteries. Positive terminal is red or marked +. Negative is black or –.
  3. Connect red to dead. Clamp one red end to the dead battery's positive terminal. Make sure the clamp bites metal, not plastic.
  4. Connect red to good. Clamp the other red end to the good battery's positive terminal.
  5. Connect black to good. Clamp a black end to the good battery's negative terminal.
  6. Ground the last black clamp. Clamp it to bare metal on the dead car—engine block bracket or strut bolt. Not the battery.
  7. Start the good car. Let it run two minutes. Then start the dead car. If it won't start after a few tries, the battery may be too far gone.
  8. Disconnect in reverse. Remove black from dead car first, then black from good, then both reds. Keep clamps from touching each other.
  9. Drive. Run the revived car 20–30 minutes to recharge.

Never connect the final black clamp to the dead battery's negative post. A spark near battery gas can cause an explosion.

Parallel Park

It's geometry, not magic. Here's the sequence.

  1. Find a spot. You need about 1.5 times your car's length. Signal and pull alongside the front car, about two feet away, rear bumpers aligned.
  2. Check the mirror. Look for traffic. When clear, shift to reverse.
  3. Crank the wheel right. Turn the wheel all the way right while backing up slowly. Your car should angle toward the curb at about 45 degrees.
  4. Straighten when you see the curb. Once your car is at 45 degrees, straighten the wheel and keep backing until your front bumper clears the car ahead.
  5. Crank left. Turn the wheel all the way left and back in. Your car should swing into the spot.
  6. Fine-tune. Straighten out, center yourself, and adjust forward or back if needed.
  7. Park. Set the brake, turn off the engine, and check your spacing before opening the door.

If you're too far from the curb, pull forward and try again. Small adjustments are normal.

Poach an Egg

The trick is fresh eggs and a gentle swirl. No special pan required.

  1. Use the freshest eggs you have. Older whites spread. If you only have old eggs, add a splash of vinegar to the water.
  2. Heat water to a bare simmer. About 180°F. Small bubbles on the bottom, no rolling boil.
  3. Add a splash of vinegar. One tablespoon white vinegar helps the white coagulate. It won't affect taste.

  6. Poach 3–4 minutes. The white should be set, the yolk still runny. Lift with a slotted spoon.
  7. Drain. Rest the spoon on a paper towel for a few seconds before serving.

If the egg sticks to the bottom, your water was too hot. Lower the heat and try again.

    Brown, brittle leaves won't come back. Snip with clean scissors so the plant stops spending on them.

  3. Water from the bottom

    Set the pot in a bowl of water for 30 minutes. Roots drink upward and you avoid a soggy top layer.

  4. Let it drain fully

    Lift it out, let it drip. Standing water in a saucer rots roots.

  5. Move it to gentle light

    Bright shade, no direct sun. A recovering plant sunburns easily.

  6. Wait a week, then look

    New growth at the tips means you won. If the stem is still firm, there's hope.

Almost gone: Mushy stems at the base? Cut above the rot and try propagating a healthy cutting in water.

Thank-You Notes That Land

Three sentences. Specific beats fancy every time.

cached matchShort & warm
  1. Open with the actual thing

    "Thank you for the cast iron skillet." Naming it proves you remembered and cared.

  2. Say what it meant or how you'll use it

    "I've already made cornbread twice. It's a keeper." One concrete detail does the heavy lifting.

  3. Add a line about them

    "It was good to see you at the party." Or reference the time, the talk, the laugh.

    "Thanks again, and warm wishes." Then your name. No need for a paragraph.

  5. Sign it by hand

    Even a typed note gets a handwritten sign-off. It reads as real.

    Late is fine, just not never. The gesture still counts.

A skeleton you can steal

"Thank you so much for ___. I've been ___ and it means a lot. It was great to ___. Thanks again, — [Your name]"

Wake Up Your Coffee Maker

If the coffee tastes off, the machine is usually the culprit, not the beans.

cached match30 min
  1. Empty the reservoir and set the carafe

    Make sure the whole brew path is ready, and the carafe is where it should be.

  2. Mix 1 part white vinegar, 1 part water

    Half and half, enough to fill the reservoir. Skip scented or cleaning vinegar.

    Then let it sit 15 minutes with the hot vinegar solution in the carafe. That's where the descaling happens.

    One more cycle loosens anything stubborn in the tubes.

instances.title: dashboard_steps: Remove a Stripped Screw
user_requests: how do i get out a stripped screw
I stripped a screw and can't get it out
tips for removing a stripped screw?
need to remove stripped screw asap
instances.html:
Remove a Stripped Screw

Screws strip. Patience and a little grit get them out without wrecking the hole.

  1. Try grip first. Stretch a wide rubber band over the screw head and press your driver in hard. Turn slowly. The rubber fills the stripped slots.
  2. Upgrade the driver. Switch to a screwdriver that fits the remaining slots exactly. A #2 Phillips for most. Push in firmly while turning counterclockwise.
  3. Add downward pressure. Lean your weight into the driver so it can't cam out. Slow is fast here.
  4. Cut a new slot. If the head is exposed enough, use a rotary tool with a cutting wheel to carve a straight slot. Then use a flathead driver.
  5. Use a screw extractor. Drill a small pilot hole in the screw head, then twist in the extractor (reverse thread). It bites and backs the screw out.
  6. Last resort: drill it out. Drill through the screw head with a bit slightly smaller than the shank. The head pops off, and you can remove the rest with pliers.

Go slow. Rushing strips it more. If you feel slipping, stop and reset your grip.

instances.title: dashboard_steps: Whistle Loudly With Your Fingers
user_requests: how do you whistle using your fingers
instances.html:
Whistle Loudly With Your Fingers

It's all about the air stream and a tight seal. Once it clicks, you'll never forget.

  1. Wet your lips. Dry lips don't seal. A quick lick helps.
  2. Make a “V” with two fingers. Use your index and middle finger (or thumb and index). They'll go under your tongue.
  3. Fold your tongue back. Pull the tip of your tongue back toward your throat, creating a channel. Your fingers push the tongue back and hold it there.
  4. Place fingers under tongue. Slide them in about a knuckle deep. They should press the tongue up slightly.
  5. Close your lips around fingers. Tight seal. No air should escape around them.
  6. Blow hard. A sharp, forceful breath out. Adjust finger angle and tongue position until you get a piercing tone.

Try it. It may take a few tries. If you get a weak hiss, blow harder and press fingers deeper.

instances.title: dashboard_steps: Get Rid of Fruit Flies
user_requests: get rid of fruit flies naturally
how do i get rid of fruit flies
instances.html:
Get Rid of Fruit Flies

They breed in drains and overripe produce. Break the cycle and they vanish.

  1. Find the source. Check fruit bowls, compost, trash, and sink drains. Fruit flies lay eggs in fermenting stuff.
  2. Clean drains. Pour boiling water down the drain, then follow with a baking soda and vinegar mix. Let it sit, then flush.
  3. Make a trap. Put a splash of apple cider vinegar in a jar. Add a drop of dish soap. Cover with plastic wrap and poke small holes. Flies go in, can't get out.
  4. Refrigerate produce. Any ripe fruit goes in the fridge until the flies are gone.
  5. Take out trash daily. Especially anything sweet or rotting.
  6. Repeat. Keep traps out for a week after you stop seeing flies. Eggs hatch fast.

Don't skip the drain. That's where most infestations hide.

instances.title: dashboard_steps: Clean a Whiteboard
instances.html:
Clean a Whiteboard

Regular cleaning keeps it bright. Ghost marks mean it's time for a deeper clean.

  1. Erase thoroughly. Use a clean eraser. Wipe in one direction, not circles, to avoid smears.
  2. Spray with whiteboard cleaner. Or use a 50/50 mix of water and isopropyl alcohol. Spray a small section.
  3. Wipe with a microfiber cloth. Work top to bottom. Rinse the cloth as it gets dirty.
  4. For stubborn marks, use a magic eraser. Dampen it and gently scrub. Don't press too hard; it can dull the surface.
  5. Rinse with clean water. Remove all cleaner residue. Dry with a clean cloth.
  6. Season if new. Before first use, write over the whole board with a whiteboard marker, erase, and repeat. This primes it.

Never use abrasive cleaners. They scratch the surface and make future cleaning harder.

instances.title: dashboard_steps: Get Gum Out of Hair
user_requests: how to remove gum from hair
get gum out of hair without cutting
gum in my hair what do i do
instances.html:
Get Gum Out of Hair

Don't reach for scissors yet. Oil, ice, or peanut butter usually does the trick.

  1. Ice it first. Hold an ice cube on the gum for a few minutes. It freezes and becomes brittle. Pick at it gently; it may crumble out.
  2. Try oil. Massage a little olive oil, baby oil, or peanut butter into the gum and hair. Let it sit 5 minutes. The oil breaks down the gum's stickiness.
  3. Comb it out. Use a fine-tooth comb. Start at the ends of the gum and work inward. Be patient.
  4. Wash hair. Once the gum is out, shampoo well to remove the oil.
  5. If all else fails, cut. As a last resort, cut the gum out with small scissors, trying to keep as much hair as possible.

Don't pull. Yanking spreads the gum and hurts. Work slowly.

instances.title: dashboard_steps: Sharpen a Kitchen Knife
instances.html:
Sharpen a Kitchen Knife

A sharp knife is safer. Ten minutes with a whetstone brings it back.

  1. Soak the whetstone. If it's a water stone, submerge it for 10–15 minutes. If it's oil, skip.
  2. Find the angle. Most kitchen knives are 15–20 degrees per side. That's roughly the height of two stacked coins under the spine.
  3. Start on the coarse side. Place the blade at the angle. Push away from you, maintaining angle. Do 10 passes per side.
  4. Flip and repeat. Do the same number on the other side.
  5. Move to the fine side. Repeat with lighter pressure. This polishes the edge.
  6. Test. Slice a piece of paper. If it cuts cleanly, you're done. If not, repeat a few more passes.

Keep the angle steady. Consistency matters more than pressure.

instances.title: dashboard_steps: Replace a Toilet Paper Roll in a Charming Old House

instances.html:
Replace a Toilet Paper Roll

Small task, real satisfaction. Let's do it cleanly, user_name.

  1. Notice the holder type. Spring-loaded bar? Just compress it and lift one end. Fixed spindle? Pull the spindle out sideways.
  2. Slide the empty tube off and drop it in the recycling, not the floor.
  3. Mount the new roll so paper feeds over the top. Looks neat and is genuinely easier to grab.
  4. Seat the spring bar back in both cups until you feel it click.
  5. Give it a test pull. One sheet. If the roll spins free or the paper tears sideways, the bar isn't seated.
The over vs. under debate

Over is the standard, and yes, older patents back that up. If you're in a home that insists on under, you have my sympathy and respect.

If the roll keeps falling off mid-pull, the spring has lost tension. A small rubber band inside the bar buys you a few more weeks before replacement.

instances.title: dashboard_steps: Load a Dishwasher So Everything Actually Gets Clean
user_requests: how to load a dishwasher correctly
why does my dishwasher leave food on plates
how to stack dishes in the dishwasher
teach me to load the dishwasher like a pro
instances.html:
Load a Dishwasher Properly

Most dishwasher disappointment is a loading problem, not a machine problem.

  1. Scrape, don't rinse. Modern detergents need food residue to work. A quick scrape is all you owe it.
  2. Bottom rack, back to front: plates and serving dishes, facing the center so spray reaches the dirty surface.
  3. Top rack, angled down: glasses and cups upside down, tilted slightly so water can't pool in the bottoms.
  4. Utensil basket: sharp knives point down, spoons and forks mixed pointing up and down so they don't nest.
  5. Never block the spray arm and don't stack anything in front of the detergent door.
  6. Run hot water at the sink until it's warm before starting, so the first rinse isn't cold.
What should never go in

Cast iron, most good knives, wooden spoons, and antique china with gold trim. Hand-wash those and stay friends with them.

Plastic containers flip and fill with water. Anchor them on the top rack under a heavy cup or accept the swimming pool.

laundrey advice for someone who ruins everything
instances.html:
Do Laundry Without Shrinking Anything

Two rules solve 90% of laundry disasters, user_name: read the tag, and respect heat.

  1. Read the care tag on the item you're least sure about. It usually knows better than you do.
  2. Sort into three piles: lights, darks, and things you'd cry over.
  3. Check pockets and zip zippers. Zipped zippers don't snag, empty pockets don't ruin the drum.
  4. Cold water for everything except towels and sheets. Cold prevents both shrinking and colour bleed.
  5. Turn knits and prints inside out. This protects the surface where pilling and fading show first.
  6. Dry on low or air-dry. Heat is the shrinking culprit, full stop.
If it's already shrunk

Soak the item in cool water with a cap of hair conditioner for 20 minutes, then gently stretch it back to shape and lay flat to dry. It sometimes works, which is better than never.

Wool and cashmere: hand-wash cool, press water out with a towel, dry flat. Never hang a wet sweater. Gravity does not negotiate.

instances.title: dashboard_steps: Charge a Dead Phone Battery Faster
user_requests: how to charge my phone faster
why is my phone charging so slow
my phone charges slow what do i do
instances.html:
Charge a Phone Battery Faster

Charging speed is mostly about heat and the right brick. Here's the short version.

  1. Use the charger that came in the box or one rated for your phone's fast-charge standard. A random gas-station brick wins nothing.
  2. Skip the car and the laptop ports. They trickle. Fine overnight, slow when you need it.
  3. Take the case off if it's thick. Trapped heat throttles charging speed.
  4. Don't use it while it charges unless you must. Screen on plus juice flowing equals slower fill and a warm battery.
  5. Turn on airplane mode if you're in a hurry. Cutting the radios gets you a noticeable bump.
  6. Recharge between 20% and 80% on most days rather than draining to zero. Lithium cells age kinder that way.
Is the cable the problem?

Often, yes. Cables fray internally before they look ruined. Swap in a known-good cable before blaming the phone.

If the phone gets hot enough to notice while charging, stop and let it cool. Heat is what actually kills batteries.

Return an Online Order

Returns are a paperwork sport. Move through the steps in order and it's painless.

  1. Find the return window in your order confirmation email or account page. It's usually 30 days from delivery.
  2. Start the return in your account, not by email, so you get a tracking number in writing.
  3. Pick the reason honestly. \"Changed my mind\" is fine. Lying about damage gets returns rejected.
  4. Print the label or save the QR code. No printer? Most drop-off points scan a code from your phone.
  5. Repack in the original box with tags and accessories. Anything missing can trim your refund.
  6. Keep the drop-off receipt until the refund lands. If it vanishes, that slip is your evidence.
Who pays shipping?

Defective or wrong item: they do. Changed your mind: usually you do, often deducted from the refund. Check before you ship.

Refunds take 3-10 business days after the warehouse scans the package. If it's day 14, that's when you email, user_name.

user_requests: how to cook rice without a rice cooker
my rice always comes out mushy
rice keeps sticking to the pan help
instances.html:
Cook Rice on the Stove

No cooker required. Ratio, lid, and patience, user_name.

  1. Rinse the rice in cool water until the water runs mostly clear. This is the anti-sticky step.
  2. Use 1 part rice to 1.75 parts water for long-grain white. Add a pinch of salt.
  3. Bring to a boil uncovered, then drop to the lowest simmer your stove can hold.
  4. Clamp the lid on and don't peek or stir. Steam is doing the work now.
  5. Simmer 15 minutes, then take it off the heat and let it sit covered for 10 more.
  6. Fluff with a fork, not a spoon. Fork tines separate grains; spoons mash them.
Brown rice and other grains

Brown rice needs about 2.25 parts water and 40-45 minutes. Basmati and jasmine follow the white rice timing, just with a rinse and a shorter soak.

Rice stuck to the bottom of the pot? You stirred it. Now you know. Serve from the top and soak the pan before scrubbing.

user_requests: how do i chill a beer fast
quickest way to get a warm soda cold

instances.html:
Chill a Drink in 5 Minutes

No ice? No problem. Physics is on your side, user_name.

  1. Wrap it wet. Soak a paper towel, wring it slightly, and wrap the can or bottle.
  2. Freezer, not fridge. Fridge adds hours. Freezer does the work in minutes.
  3. Add salt to the ice bath. Saltwater melts colder than plain water, so it pulls heat out faster.
  4. Spin, don't stare. Roll the can between your palms every minute. Moving liquid meets more cold surface.
  5. Five minutes, tops. Longer and you risk a burst can or a slushy mess.
Song reference

Put on one good song and rotate your drink once per chorus.

instances.title: dashboard_steps: Tie a Tie (Four-in-Hand)

instances.html:
Tie a Tie: Four-in-Hand

The knot that forgives, user_name.

  1. Drape the tie around your neck, wide end on your right, hanging about a foot lower than the narrow end.
  2. Cross the wide end over the narrow one.
  3. Loop the wide end back underneath, toward your neck.
  4. Bring the wide end across the front, left to right.
  5. Pull it up through the loop at your neck.
  6. Thread it down through the knot you just made.
  7. Hold the narrow end, slide the knot up, and tighten gently. Dimple optional, charm mandatory.
Sizing check

Knot should sit at your collar, tip at your belt buckle.

instances.html:
Fold a Fitted Sheet

Yes, it can be done. Even by you, user_name.

  1. Lay it inside-out on the bed, elastic up.
  2. Put your hands into two corners, then fold one corner into the other, tucking the first inside the second.
  3. Do the same on the other end, so you have two corner pockets.
  4. Lay it flat and fold one pocket over the other, corners nesting.
  5. Smooth it into a rectangle with your hands.
  6. Fold in thirds lengthwise, then in thirds again.
  7. Stand it up in the closet instead of stacking. It salutes you.
If it's still lumpy

Perfect is optional. A flat-ish rectangle still fits the shelf.

best way to write a to-do
instances.html:
Write a To-Do List You Actually Finish

Fewer things, more done, user_name.

  1. Brain dump first. Every task onto paper, no order, no judgment.
  2. Pick three. Circle the ones that matter today. Three is a list; twelve is a wish.
  3. Verbs first. "Email Sam the draft," not "Sam stuff."
  4. Add a size. Mark each as 5 min, 30 min, or "whole afternoon."
  5. Start with the smallest. Momentum is cheaper than motivation.
  6. Leave one blank slot. A gap is where real life lands.
  7. Tonight, cross off or carry. Anything carried three days gets cut or scheduled.
One rule

If it takes under two minutes, do it now instead of writing it down.

instances.title: dashboard_steps: Brew Better Cold Brew at Home
user_requests: how to make cold brew coffee
cold brew at home without a gadget
instances.html:
Brew Better Cold Brew

Low effort, big payoff, user_name.

  1. Coarse grind. Like raw sugar. Fine grounds turn muddy and bitter.
  2. Ratio: 1 cup grounds to 4 cups cold water in a jar or pitcher.
  3. Stir once so every ground gets wet. No dry islands.
  4. Cover and wait 12–18 hours at room temp. Longer means stronger, not better.
  5. Strain twice. Once through a sieve, once through a paper filter or cloth.
  6. Store the concentrate in the fridge up to a week.
  7. Serve 1 part concentrate to 2 parts water or milk over ice. Adjust until it tastes like yours.
Too bitter?

Shorten the steep or dilute more. Bitterness is time and heat, not fate.

instances.title: dashboard_steps: Wrap a Gift Without Losing the Tape
instances.html:
Wrap a Gift Without Losing the Tape

Paper, tape, patience. In that order, user_name.

  1. Tape the tape. Stick a strip to the table edge so it's findable, not lost in the paper.
  2. Measure first. Paper should wrap around with about 2 inches of overlap.
  3. Cut straight. One clean line beats three ragged ones.
  4. Center, flip, fold. Box face-down on the paper, pull one side over, tape it.
  5. Fold the ends. Crease the corners into triangles, then fold them in like a hospital corner.
  6. Tape the seams flat, pressing as you go.
  7. Skip the bow if you want. A plain ribbon or a doodle on the tag is plenty.
Odd shapes

Soft or round items: wrap in tissue first, then treat it like a box.
